case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal prisoner who cannot file a second or successive § 2255 motion may use § 2255(e)’s “saving clause” to seek habeas relief under § 2241 based on an intervening Supreme Court statutory-interpretation decision (Rehaif) that allegedly renders his § 922(g) conviction invalid.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2255(e) (the “saving clause,” permitting resort to habeas under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 when the § 2255 remedy is “inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention”), in interaction with § 2255(h) (limits on second/successive motions), and the underlying criminal statutes 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) and 18 U.S.C. § 924(e)(1).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Jones argues that after Rehaif v. United States clarified that § 922(g) requires proof the defendant knew of his prohibited status, his conviction is legally invalid; because circuit precedent foreclosed that argument when he filed his first § 2255 motion and § 2255(h) does not allow a successive motion based on a new statutory-interpretation rule, § 2255 is “inadequate or ineffective” to test the legality of his detention, so the saving clause should allow him to bring the claim in a § 2241 habeas petition.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government argues that § 2255 is not “inadequate or ineffective” merely because a prisoner cannot satisfy § 2255(h)’s gatekeeping requirements; the saving clause is narrow and does not authorize end-runs around the limits Congress imposed on second/successive collateral attacks, so Rehaif-based statutory claims like Jones’s must be brought (if at all) through § 2255 and cannot be re-routed through § 2241 via § 2255(e).
key_precedents: Rehaif v. United States, 139 S. Ct. 2191 (2019)
Jones v. Hendrix, 8 F.4th 683 (8th Cir. 2021) (decision below)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s miscarriage-of-justice argument is the most powerful equitable objection, but under the text § 2255(e) asks whether the motion remedy is “inadequate or ineffective to test” legality—not whether AEDPA’s successive-motion limits in § 2255(h) foreclose relitigation after one full opportunity. Justice Jackson’s contention that circuit precedent plus § 2255(h) meant there was never a meaningful “test” effectively converts unfavorable law into “inadequacy,” which would swallow § 2255(h) and make the saving clause an alternate successive-review track. Hayman, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, supports a forum/process-focused understanding of the saving clause—preserving § 2241 for situations where the sentencing court cannot entertain the motion or the mechanism cannot function—not for later statutory-interpretation developments Congress chose not to include in § 2255(h). A narrow holding for respondent—limited to claims barred solely by § 2255(h), without opining on true structural impossibility cases—best respects the enacted scheme and institutional finality.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest point: that when circuit precedent foreclosed a Rehaif-type claim on the first § 2255 motion and § 2255(h) blocks a second, the prisoner never meaningfully “tested” the legality of his detention. But on the statute’s original public meaning, “test” refers to the availability of the § 2255 remedial vehicle as a forum to adjudicate legality, not a guarantee of success or a later opportunity whenever statutory interpretation changes; as Justice Kagan and the Chief note, equating AEDPA’s gatekeeping with “inadequate or ineffective” would largely nullify § 2255(h) and invert the statute’s structure. Hayman supports this channeling understanding: § 2241 remains for situations where the § 2255 mechanism cannot function (e.g., practical or structural impediments), not as an escape hatch from Congress’s deliberate limits on second-or-successive motions. The miscarriage-of-justice concern is a policy argument for Congress, and absent a demonstrated Suspension Clause violation, it cannot justify rewriting § 2255(e) to supply review that § 2255(h) withholds.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest point: that when circuit precedent foreclosed a claim on the first § 2255 motion and § 2255(h) bars a second, the legality of detention has not been meaningfully “tested,” risking continued incarceration for arguably non-criminal conduct. But as the Chief and Justice Kagan explain, the saving clause’s text focuses on whether the § 2255 remedial vehicle is incapable of functioning as a forum—not whether Congress has chosen, through AEDPA’s successive-motion limits, to withhold a second chance to litigate certain statutory claims. Hayman’s concern with practical breakdowns in the substitute forum (e.g., inability to access the sentencing court or obtain a hearing at all) does not support converting § 2255(e) into a merits-based escape hatch whenever later statutory interpretation shifts; that reading would substantially nullify § 2255(h) and undermine finality in a way Congress plainly contemplated. Whatever the equitable appeal of a “miscarriage of justice” safety valve, the proper source for that expansion is Congress, not judicial revision of “inadequate or ineffective” to mean “now barred under § 2255(h).”

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan make the strongest textual-structural point that § 2255(e) targets inadequacy of the remedial vehicle, not dissatisfaction with § 2255(h)’s limits, and I take seriously their concern about nullifying AEDPA’s gatekeeping. But that framing assumes the prisoner had a meaningful chance to “test the legality” in the first § 2255 motion; where binding circuit precedent made the claim legally unavailable then and § 2255(h) makes it procedurally unavailable now, the substitute remedy fails in operation for a narrow class of statutory-innocence claims. Hayman’s channeling rationale supports preserving § 2241 as a safety valve when the § 2255 substitute “preclude[s] a necessary hearing,” and my pragmatic approach cannot treat continued incarceration for potentially non-criminal conduct as a mere “second bite” problem. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern is real, but Congress’s choice of broad saving-clause language (“inadequate or ineffective”) is best read to preserve a limited miscarriage-of-justice pathway rather than a one-way ratchet that forecloses any forum to contest legality.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: that binding circuit precedent plus § 2255(h) can leave a Rehaif-type statutory innocence claim without any later forum, so legality was never meaningfully “tested.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 2255(e) asks whether the motion remedy is inadequate or ineffective as a remedial vehicle to test legality, not whether Congress later restricted successive relitigation after that vehicle was available once; treating AEDPA’s successive limits as “inadequacy” would largely collapse § 2255(h) and create an administratively incoherent, circuit-dependent bypass. Hayman does not change that conclusion for me: it describes § 2255 as an adequate substitute so long as the sentencing-court mechanism can entertain motions in the ordinary course, reserving § 2241 for structural/practical breakdowns, not for claims Congress chose not to authorize in successive collateral review. Absent a demonstrated Suspension Clause problem (which Boumediene cannot supply merely because AEDPA is strict), the statute’s coherent reading is that § 2255(e) is not an escape hatch from § 2255(h)’s substantive gatekeeping.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor press the hardest point: where circuit precedent made a Rehaif-type statutory claim futile on the first § 2255 motion and § 2255(h) bars a second, it feels like legality was never meaningfully “tested.” But as the Chief and Justice Kagan emphasize, the saving clause’s text turns on whether the § 2255 remedial vehicle is “inadequate or ineffective” as a substitute forum, not whether Congress later limited successive merits review; treating AEDPA’s gatekeeping as “inadequacy” would largely nullify § 2255(h) and invert the statute’s structure. Hayman reinforces that § 2255(e) is aimed at situations where the sentencing-court mechanism cannot function (practical/structural obstacles), not where the prisoner cannot satisfy Congress’s second-or-successive authorization. However troubling the equities, on a textualist/originalist account the remedy for any perceived gap for statutory-innocence claims lies with Congress, not with judicial expansion of § 2241 beyond the limits § 2255(e) sets.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is the fairness/miscarriage-of-justice concern: when circuit precedent foreclosed a Rehaif-type claim on the first § 2255 motion and § 2255(h) now blocks a second, the prisoner may never receive a merits determination on statutory innocence. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 2255(e)’s saving clause turns on whether the § 2255 remedial vehicle is structurally or practically incapable of functioning as the substitute forum, not whether Congress has chosen to limit successive merits review through § 2255(h). Hayman supports that channeling design: it preserves § 2241 for breakdowns in the mechanism (e.g., the sentencing court cannot entertain the motion), not as an escape hatch whenever later statutory interpretation improves the merits. Under a precedent- and text-centered approach, expanding “inadequate or ineffective” to mean “barred by AEDPA’s successive-motion limits” would effectively rewrite § 2255(h) and destabilize finality in a circuit-dependent way, leaving any gap for Congress to address.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s miscarriage-of-justice point has moral force, but the textual question is whether the § 2255 “remedy by motion” is “inadequate or ineffective to test” legality, and a bar on successive motions in § 2255(h) reflects Congress’s substantive limits—not a failure of the remedial vehicle to conduct a test. Hayman, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, describes § 2255 as a substitute for habeas that preserves § 2241 for unusual situations where the sentencing-court forum or mechanism cannot function, not as a bypass whenever later statutory interpretation would change the merits. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Boumediene-style adequacy concerns cannot override the ordinary public meaning of § 2255(e) in a context where Congress provided an initial § 2255 opportunity and then deliberately restricted successive litigation. Reading the saving clause to allow Rehaif-based claims whenever circuit precedent previously foreclosed them would effectively nullify § 2255(h)’s gatekeeping and is inconsistent with the statute’s structure.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is structural: if § 2255(e) opens whenever § 2255(h) bars a successive motion, we risk collapsing AEDPA’s gatekeeping into a parallel § 2241 track. But that framing treats the initial § 2255 opportunity as a meaningful “test” even when binding precedent made the statutory-innocence claim legally unavailable at the time, and § 2255(h) later makes it procedurally unavailable—so in operation there has been no real adjudicative testing of the detention’s legality in the sense Hayman contemplated (a “necessary hearing”). Under a pragmatic, fairness-centered approach, I read “inadequate or ineffective” to capture this narrow circumstance where the substitute remedy fails to provide any forum to litigate a non-criminality claim, without authorizing broad relitigation of ordinary statutory changes. Justice Barrett’s concern that this rewrites § 2255(h) is serious, but I see it as giving effect to § 2255(e)’s independent safety-valve text rather than nullifying Congress’s limits, because the clause is triggered only when the system has functionally foreclosed any first merits consideration of legal innocence.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 2255(e)’s saving clause preserves resort to § 2241 only when the § 2255 motion remedy is structurally “inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention,” not when the prisoner’s claim is merely barred by Congress’s limits on second-or-successive motions in § 2255(h). Reading the saving clause to permit Rehaif-based statutory claims whenever circuit precedent previously foreclosed them would create an end-run around § 2255(h) and undermine the careful gatekeeping scheme Congress enacted, inviting broad relitigation and harming institutional finality. United States v. Hayman describes § 2255’s purpose as channeling collateral review to the sentencing court while keeping habeas available when § 2255 cannot provide a meaningful forum (e.g., practical impediments to adjudication), not as a mechanism to override statutory limits on successive petitions. A narrow ruling for the government best respects the text and structure of § 2255(e) and § 2255(h), preserves precedent, and avoids destabilizing collateral review across the federal system.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 2255(e) makes § 2255 the exclusive postconviction vehicle unless the motion remedy is "inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner's] detention," and inability to satisfy § 2255(h)’s limits on second or successive motions does not render the remedy itself inadequate—it reflects Congress’s deliberate choice to restrict repetitive collateral attacks. Reading the saving clause to permit § 2241 whenever a new statutory-interpretation decision (like Rehaif) is unavailable under § 2255(h) would nullify § 2255(h)’s gatekeeping and convert the exception into the rule, contrary to the statute’s structure and ordinary meaning. United States v. Hayman confirms § 2255 was enacted as a substitute for habeas to channel claims to the sentencing court, with the saving clause aimed at unusual circumstances where the § 2255 forum/process cannot function (e.g., inability to obtain a necessary hearing), not as an avenue to evade Congress’s successive-motion limits. Because Jones could “test” his detention through an initial § 2255 motion even if circuit precedent made success unlikely, § 2255 was not “inadequate or ineffective” within the meaning of § 2255(e).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of § 2255(e) makes § 2241 available only when the § 2255 remedy is truly “inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention,” not merely when the prisoner cannot satisfy Congress’s strict limits on second or successive motions in § 2255(h). Reading the saving clause to cover Rehaif-based statutory claims would nullify § 2255(h)’s gatekeeping scheme and invite an end-run around AEDPA’s finality rules, with serious practical consequences for law enforcement and the administration of criminal justice. United States v. Hayman confirms that § 2255 was designed to channel collateral review to the sentencing court while preserving habeas only for situations where the § 2255 remedy is structurally unavailable—not to reopen final convictions whenever later statutory-interpretation decisions emerge. Whatever Rehaif changed about § 922(g), Congress did not authorize successive § 2255 litigation on that basis, and § 2255(e) should not be expanded to do so indirectly.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2255(e) preserves access to habeas under § 2241 when the § 2255 motion remedy is “inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention,” and it is inadequate when binding circuit precedent previously foreclosed a statutory-innocence claim and § 2255(h) now bars any successive motion to raise it. After Rehaif v. United States clarified that § 922(g) requires knowledge of prohibited status, a prisoner who may be legally innocent must have some meaningful vehicle to test that detention; reading the saving clause to shut the courthouse door would risk the “complete miscarriage of justice” condemned in Davis v. United States. United States v. Hayman confirms § 2255 was enacted to channel, not to extinguish, habeas, and it emphasized that where § 2255 would otherwise preclude a necessary hearing, the saving clause keeps habeas “open” to afford that hearing. Construing § 2255(e) to permit § 2241 here best harmonizes the text with § 2255’s historic purpose and avoids imprisoning people for conduct Congress did not make criminal merely because of a procedural trap created by intervening statutory interpretation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2255(e)’s saving clause turns on whether the “remedy by motion is inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention,” and the most natural reading is that it addresses defects in the § 2255 remedial vehicle (e.g., inability of the sentencing court to entertain the motion), not disagreement with the substantive limits Congress imposed on successive collateral review in § 2255(h). Allowing Rehaif-based statutory-interpretation claims to proceed under § 2241 whenever § 2255(h) bars a second motion would largely nullify § 2255(h)’s careful gatekeeping and create an unworkable, circuit-dependent end run around AEDPA’s design. United States v. Hayman underscores that § 2255 was enacted to channel federal prisoners’ collateral attacks into the sentencing court while preserving habeas only where § 2255 cannot practically or legally do the job, not to expand collateral review whenever later statutory interpretation favors the prisoner. Rehaif may show a legal error, but Congress chose in § 2255(h) not to authorize successive motions for new statutory rules, and § 2255(e) should not be read to undo that choice.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2255(e)’s saving clause allows resort to § 2241 only when “the remedy by motion is inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention,” and the most natural reading is that it concerns the availability of a forum to adjudicate a § 2255 motion—not whether the movant can satisfy § 2255(h)’s limits on second or successive motions. Accepting petitioner’s view would effectively nullify § 2255(h) by permitting prisoners to bypass Congress’s carefully drawn gatekeeping rules whenever an intervening statutory-interpretation decision (like Rehaif) supplies a new argument. United States v. Hayman confirms § 2255 was designed to channel collateral attacks through the sentencing court while preserving habeas only for unusual situations where the § 2255 mechanism cannot be used, not to create an alternative track whenever later law changes. The separation of powers counsels respecting the limits Congress enacted in AEDPA and not expanding § 2255(e) beyond its text to create a broader successive-review regime the statute does not provide.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 2255(e)’s saving clause preserves resort to § 2241 only when the § 2255 motion remedy is structurally “inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention,” not when the prisoner merely cannot satisfy Congress’s gatekeeping limits on second or successive motions in § 2255(h). Reading the saving clause to allow Rehaif-based statutory claims whenever prior circuit precedent foreclosed them would create an end-run around § 2255(h) and undermine AEDPA’s finality-focused design, a practical and institutional concern. Hayman indicates the clause exists to ensure a meaningful forum when § 2255 cannot function as a substitute for habeas (e.g., inability to obtain a necessary hearing), not to reopen convictions whenever later statutory-interpretation decisions arise. Because Jones’s inability to file a successive § 2255 motion stems from § 2255(h)’s deliberate limits rather than any failure of the § 2255 forum to “test” legality, § 2241 is unavailable.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 2255(e) preserves recourse to § 2241 only when the § 2255 motion remedy is structurally “inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention,” not when the prisoner is simply barred by § 2255(h)’s limits on second or successive motions. Reading the saving clause to allow Rehaif-based statutory claims whenever circuit precedent once foreclosed them would nullify Congress’s gatekeeping choices in § 2255(h) and undermine the finality AEDPA sought to secure. United States v. Hayman confirms § 2255 was designed to replace traditional habeas for federal prisoners while leaving § 2241 available for unusual circumstances where the § 2255 forum or mechanism cannot provide a meaningful test—not as a backdoor to relitigate merits after failing § 2255(h). Because Jones’s claim challenges the correctness of his conviction under an intervening statutory-interpretation decision rather than demonstrating any inability of the § 2255 procedure to function as a remedial vehicle, § 2255 is not “inadequate or ineffective” within the meaning of § 2255(e).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2255(e) allows resort to § 2241 when the § 2255 motion remedy is “inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention,” and a Rehaif-based claim that the Government failed to prove the required knowledge element is quintessentially a challenge to the legality of detention. Under United States v. Hayman, the saving clause preserves habeas when § 2255’s operation would otherwise preclude a meaningful hearing on a claim that would have been cognizable in habeas, and § 2255(h)’s gatekeeping—by excluding new statutory-interpretation decisions—can leave a prisoner with no forum to test a potentially non-criminal conviction. Reading the saving clause to cover this narrow circumstance respects Congress’s channeling of collateral review to the sentencing court while avoiding the practical and fairness consequences of continued imprisonment for conduct that, as properly interpreted, may not be criminal. This approach also accords with the Court’s understanding (e.g., Boumediene’s reliance on the saving clause) that § 2255 must not be construed to narrow habeas’s historic function without an adequate substitute.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal prisoner who cannot satisfy AEDPA’s limits on second-or-successive § 2255 motions may use § 2255(e)’s “saving clause” to file a § 2241 habeas petition raising a Rehaif-based claim that his § 922(g) conviction is invalid.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2255(e) (the “saving clause”), in relation to 28 U.S.C. § 2255(h) (limits on second-or-successive motions) and the underlying conviction statute 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) (as interpreted in Rehaif v. United States).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Jones argues that § 2255 is “inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of his detention” within the meaning of § 2255(e) when controlling circuit precedent at the time of his first § 2255 motion foreclosed his Rehaif-type claim, and AEDPA later bars a second § 2255 motion to raise it; therefore, the saving clause should permit him to proceed via § 2241 to challenge the legality of his conviction based on an intervening statutory-interpretation decision.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government argues that § 2255 is not “inadequate or ineffective” merely because AEDPA prevents raising a claim in a second-or-successive § 2255 motion; the saving clause is limited to unusual situations where § 2255 cannot practically provide a forum (e.g., the sentencing court is unavailable), not to cases where a prisoner’s claim is procedurally barred, and allowing § 2241 here would undermine Congress’s deliberate restrictions in § 2255(h).
key_precedents: Rehaif v. United States, 139 S. Ct. 2191 (2019)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor press the hardest point: the present-tense “is inadequate or ineffective” and the fairness/Suspension Clause concern when intervening statutory precedent reveals a potentially unlawful conviction yet § 2255(h) bars a successive motion. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, the text and structure tie “inadequate or ineffective” to the remedial vehicle’s capacity to function, not to Congress’s deliberate decision to limit successive claims; otherwise the saving clause would largely undo § 2255(h) and re-create broad § 2241 habeas for statutory-interpretation changes. Hayman’s account reinforces that § 2255(e) is a narrow safety valve for unusual unavailability of the sentencing-court remedy, not an equitable override of AEDPA’s gatekeeping. Under a minimalist approach, I would hold only that inability to satisfy § 2255(h) does not by itself make § 2255 “inadequate or ineffective,” reserving any true Suspension Clause edge case for a record where § 2255 offers no meaningful opportunity at all.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the present-tense phrasing—§ 2255(e) asks whether the remedy “is inadequate or ineffective” now, and they argue that when circuit precedent once foreclosed the claim and § 2255(h) bars a second motion, the prisoner has no meaningful forum. But on a textual and structural reading, “remedy by motion” refers to the § 2255 mechanism’s capacity to adjudicate legality in the sentencing court, not whether Congress has chosen to restrict successive uses of that mechanism; treating AEDPA’s gatekeeping as “inadequacy” would, as Chief Justice Roberts explains, largely collapse § 2255(h) and convert the saving clause into a general bypass for intervening statutory decisions. Hayman supports the narrower understanding that the saving clause addresses unusual situations where the § 2255 forum cannot practically function, not where Congress has imposed finality limits that make a particular claim procedurally unavailable. Boumediene-style “meaningful opportunity” concerns, while serious, cannot justify rewriting § 2255(e)’s text; any Suspension Clause issue would have to be confronted directly rather than by expanding “inadequate or ineffective” beyond its ordinary public meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is the practical one: if circuit precedent foreclosed the claim on the first § 2255 motion and § 2255(h) bars a second, the prisoner lacks a present forum and may be legally innocent, raising Suspension Clause anxieties. But § 2255(e)’s text asks whether the “remedy by motion” is inadequate or ineffective to test legality in the structural sense—i.e., whether § 2255 can function as the vehicle—rather than whether Congress has limited successive use of that vehicle, and reading it otherwise would, as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, largely nullify § 2255(h)’s gatekeeping. Hayman supports that channeling purpose and the narrow safety valve for unusual unavailability of the sentencing-court forum, not an exception whenever AEDPA’s limits foreclose relief. Boumediene’s “meaningful opportunity” language does not justify rewriting § 2255(e) to override Congress’s successive-motion limits; any constitutional backstop would have to be addressed directly, and this case does not warrant expanding the saving clause beyond its ordinary meaning.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point seriously: if § 2255(e) opens whenever § 2255(h) blocks a successive motion, we risk undermining AEDPA’s gatekeeping and finality interests. But as Justice Jackson underscores, that framing collapses the saving clause into near-irrelevance precisely when a prisoner can no longer “test the legality” of detention in any meaningful, present-tense sense—especially where binding circuit precedent made the claim unavailable on the first motion and § 2255(h) now forecloses any second. Hayman’s channeling rationale, invoked by Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett, matters, yet Hayman also rests § 2255’s legitimacy on being an adequate substitute for habeas; when the substitute categorically cannot entertain a potentially meritorious statutory-innocence claim, the safety valve must have limited force to avoid the intolerable real-world consequence of continued imprisonment without any forum. A narrow rule confined to claims previously foreclosed by binding precedent and later validated by an intervening statutory decision addresses Roberts’s “end-run” concern while honoring Boumediene’s meaningful-opportunity principle and basic fairness to those most vulnerable to wrongful detention.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s present-tense point—“is inadequate or ineffective”—forcefully highlights the real-world gap when circuit law previously foreclosed a claim and § 2255(h) now blocks a second motion. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, reading that gap as “inadequacy” would make § 2255(e) a general workaround for AEDPA’s successive-motion limits, substantially undoing § 2255(h) and disrupting the statute’s coherent channeling design described in Hayman. Textually, “remedy by motion” speaks to the vehicle’s capacity and availability, not whether Congress has chosen to restrict repeat use of that vehicle for certain claims; a remedy is not “ineffective” simply because it is limited. To the extent Boumediene/Suspension Clause concerns remain, I agree with Roberts that they should be confronted as constitutional edge cases rather than by expanding the saving clause beyond its ordinary remedial sense.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the present-tense, practical claim that after intervening statutory precedent and § 2255(h)’s bar, the prisoner has no meaningful forum, raising serious Suspension Clause anxieties under Boumediene’s “meaningful opportunity” framing. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, the saving clause’s text asks whether the “remedy by motion” is inadequate or ineffective as a remedial vehicle—not whether Congress has made a particular claim noncognizable in a successive motion—and treating AEDPA’s gatekeeping as “inadequacy” would largely nullify § 2255(h) by turning every new statutory-interpretation decision into a § 2241 gateway. Hayman, as Justice Thomas notes, supports a narrow safety valve for situations where the § 2255 mechanism cannot practically function (forum/availability problems), not as an escape hatch whenever later law makes a claim newly attractive but Congress has chosen finality. If a true Suspension Clause edge case exists, it should be addressed as a constitutional question on an appropriate record, not by rewriting § 2255(e)’s ordinary meaning to override § 2255(h).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the most forceful equity/Suspension Clause point: a prisoner whose claim was previously foreclosed by circuit precedent and is now barred by § 2255(h) may lack any present forum to test the legality of detention. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 2255(e) is keyed to whether the § 2255 remedial vehicle is unavailable or incapable of functioning as a forum (as in Hayman’s channeling rationale), not to whether Congress has deliberately limited successive use of that vehicle through AEDPA’s gatekeeping. Reading “inadequate or ineffective” to mean “cannot satisfy § 2255(h)” would effectively re-create broad habeas via § 2241 whenever intervening statutory-interpretation precedent arises, substantially nullifying § 2255(h) and undermining the finality/administrability judgments Congress made. Under an institutionalist, precedent- and text-focused approach, the better course is to resolve only the statutory question and leave any true Suspension Clause edge case for a situation where § 2255 provides no forum at all, not merely a restricted one.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: the saving clause’s present tense (“is inadequate or ineffective”) and the concern that, after Rehaif and AEDPA’s successive-motion bar, a prisoner may lack any meaningful forum to test a potentially unlawful conviction. But on the text and structure Congress enacted, § 2255(e) speaks to the adequacy of the “remedy by motion” as a vehicle (whether it can be used to test legality in the sentencing court), not to whether a particular claim is now procedurally barred by § 2255(h); otherwise the saving clause would swallow AEDPA’s deliberate limits and create the very end-run Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito identify. Hayman supports that channeling function with a narrow safety valve for situations where the § 2255 forum cannot practically operate, not for claims that Congress has restricted on successive review. Boumediene’s “meaningful opportunity” language does not overcome the statutory text here because Congress provided a collateral-review mechanism and then cabined successive relitigation; the Suspension Clause concern cannot justify rewriting “inadequate or ineffective” to mean “unsuccessful or unavailable due to gatekeeping.”

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan make the best structural point: if “inadequate or ineffective” is triggered whenever § 2255(h) bars a successive motion, the saving clause could swallow AEDPA’s gatekeeping. But that critique assumes the only alternative is a broad bypass; I would read § 2255(e) in a tightly cabined, present-tense way that turns on whether the § 2255 remedy can actually "test" legality now for a prisoner whose claim was previously foreclosed by binding precedent and who now asserts statutory innocence after an intervening decision—precisely the situation where § 2255, as a substitute for habeas described in Hayman, fails in practical operation. Justice Thomas’s vehicle-versus-claim distinction is serious, yet it undervalues that a remedial “vehicle” that is categorically unavailable to hear a class of potentially meritorious statutory-innocence claims due to an interaction of precedent and AEDPA is functionally ineffective at present, which also heightens the Suspension Clause concerns I flagged under Boumediene’s “meaningful opportunity” principle. On a progressive pragmatic view attentive to real-world fairness and consequences, a narrow saving-clause path better reconciles text (“is”), Hayman’s adequacy premise, and constitutional avoidance than a reading that leaves legally innocent prisoners with no forum.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 2255(e) makes § 2255 the exclusive postconviction vehicle for federal prisoners unless that remedy is "inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of his detention," and, as Congress reinforced in AEDPA, § 2255(h) deliberately restricts second-or-successive motions to two narrow categories. Reading the saving clause to allow a § 2241 petition whenever circuit precedent previously foreclosed a statutory-interpretation claim (such as a Rehaif v. United States challenge to a § 922(g) conviction) would effectively nullify § 2255(h)’s limits and invite broad end-runs around Congress’s scheme, undermining institutional legitimacy and settled expectations. United States v. Hayman indicates § 2255 was designed to channel habeas claims to the sentencing court while preserving a narrow safety valve for situations where § 2255 cannot practically provide a forum, not where the prisoner is procedurally barred by AEDPA. On minimal grounds, I would hold only that § 2255 is not “inadequate or ineffective” merely because AEDPA bars a second-or-successive motion raising an intervening statutory-interpretation claim.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 2255(e) allows resort to § 2241 only when the § 2255 motion remedy is “inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention,” which refers to the adequacy of the remedial vehicle, not whether a particular claim is barred by AEDPA’s gatekeeping limits in § 2255(h). Reading the saving clause to permit § 2241 whenever new statutory-interpretation precedent (e.g., Rehaif) arises after a first § 2255 motion would functionally nullify Congress’s explicit restrictions on second-or-successive motions, contrary to the statute’s ordinary meaning and structure. United States v. Hayman confirms § 2255 was enacted to channel collateral attacks to the sentencing court while preserving habeas only for unusual situations where the § 2255 forum cannot practically provide a hearing (such as unavailability of the sentencing court), not to evade procedural limits Congress imposed. Because Jones’s inability to satisfy § 2255(h) reflects Congress’s deliberate judgment about successive litigation rather than any inadequacy of the § 2255 remedy to “test” legality, the saving clause does not apply.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of § 2255(e) preserves resort to § 2241 only when the § 2255 remedy is truly “inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention,” not when Congress has imposed gatekeeping limits on second-or-successive motions in § 2255(h). Reading the saving clause to allow § 2241 whenever AEDPA bars a successive § 2255 motion would largely nullify § 2255(h) and undermine Congress’s deliberate choice to restrict repetitive collateral attacks. As Hayman explains, § 2255 was enacted to channel federal prisoners’ challenges to the sentencing court, leaving habeas available only for unusual situations where § 2255 cannot provide a practical forum—not as an end-run around procedural limits. Rehaif is a statutory-interpretation decision, but that does not expand § 2255(e)’s narrow exception beyond its text and structure.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2255(e) permits resort to § 2241 when the § 2255 remedy “is inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of his detention,” and where binding circuit precedent foreclosed a Rehaif-type statutory claim at the time of the first § 2255 motion and AEDPA now bars a second motion under § 2255(h), the prisoner has no meaningful forum to test the legality of a conviction that may be invalid. Reading the saving clause to turn on a merely theoretical past “opportunity” ignores Congress’s present-tense command (“is”) and risks leaving potentially legally innocent people imprisoned without any mechanism to correct the error. United States v. Hayman (1952) confirms § 2255 was meant to be an adequate substitute for habeas, not a trap that forecloses review when the substitute cannot function to adjudicate legality; that understanding also avoids serious Suspension Clause concerns where no effective remedy remains. Given Rehaif’s clarification of § 922(g)’s mens rea, fairness and the real-world consequences counsel allowing § 2241 review when § 2255 cannot, as a practical and jurisdictional matter, hear the claim.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2255(e)’s saving clause preserves habeas only when the § 2255 remedy is structurally “inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention,” not when a claim is simply barred by AEDPA’s gatekeeping limits on second-or-successive motions in § 2255(h). Reading the saving clause to allow a § 2241 petition whenever intervening statutory interpretation (like Rehaif) was previously foreclosed by circuit precedent would substantially nullify Congress’s deliberate restrictions in § 2255(h) and disrupt the coherence of the postconviction scheme. United States v. Hayman explains § 2255’s purpose as a habeas-substitute designed for workability and equivalent scope, with the saving clause reserved to keep habeas available when § 2255 cannot realistically provide a forum—not to create an end-run around procedural limits. On that pragmatic, text-focused reading, § 2255 is not “inadequate or ineffective” merely because the prisoner cannot satisfy § 2255(h)’s conditions, so relief via § 2241 is unavailable here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of § 2255(e) permits resort to § 2241 only when the § 2255 “remedy by motion is inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of his detention,” and that language naturally concerns the unavailability or impracticability of the § 2255 forum—not a prisoner’s inability to satisfy Congress’s substantive and jurisdictional limits on second-or-successive motions in § 2255(h). Reading the saving clause to allow an end-run around § 2255(h) whenever later precedent makes a claim newly attractive would defeat AEDPA’s carefully drawn restrictions and undermine separation of powers by letting courts rewrite the postconviction scheme Congress enacted. United States v. Hayman confirms § 2255 was designed to channel collateral review to the sentencing court while preserving a habeas-equivalent remedy when that channel cannot function; it does not suggest that procedural bars render § 2255 “inadequate or ineffective.” Whatever the force of Rehaif for the merits of a § 922(g) conviction, it does not expand § 2255(e)’s narrow exception beyond its plain meaning to override § 2255(h)’s limits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 2255(e)’s saving clause should be read, consistent with the history and structure of § 2255, to preserve resort to § 2241 only when the § 2255 remedy is practically unavailable or incapable of providing a forum—not when a prisoner simply cannot satisfy AEDPA’s second-or-successive limits in § 2255(h). United States v. Hayman emphasized that § 2255 was enacted to channel collateral attacks to the sentencing court while keeping habeas open in unusual circumstances where the motion remedy cannot function; it did not suggest that habeas becomes available whenever § 2255’s procedural limits foreclose relief. Allowing Rehaif-based statutory-interpretation claims to proceed via § 2241 would effectively create an end-run around Congress’s deliberate restrictions in § 2255(h), undermining workability and the finality interests AEDPA sought to protect. The claim may “test the legality” of detention in a colloquial sense, but § 2255 is not rendered “inadequate or ineffective” merely because it bars successive motions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 2255(e) preserves resort to § 2241 only when the "remedy by motion" is "inadequate or ineffective to test the legality" of detention—not when a prisoner’s claim is simply barred by AEDPA’s gatekeeping limits on second-or-successive motions in § 2255(h). Reading the saving clause to allow statutory-interpretation claims whenever intervening precedent (like Rehaif) makes a conviction arguably unlawful would effectively nullify Congress’s deliberate restrictions in § 2255(h) and permit an end run around AEDPA. Methodologically, the better textual reading is that "inadequate or ineffective" concerns the availability of the § 2255 forum to test a claim (e.g., practical or jurisdictional unavailability), not the likelihood of success or the presence of procedural bars. Although Rehaif clarified § 922(g)’s mens rea element, that intervening statutory interpretation does not expand § 2255(e) beyond its limited role in the postconviction scheme.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2255(e) preserves access to habeas when the § 2255 motion remedy is “inadequate or ineffective to test the legality of [the prisoner’s] detention,” and that inquiry should be a practical, present-tense assessment of whether the prisoner has any meaningful forum to vindicate a claim that his conduct is not criminal after an intervening statutory-interpretation decision like Rehaif. When controlling circuit precedent foreclosed the claim at the time of the first § 2255 motion and § 2255(h) now bars a successive motion, reading the saving clause to provide no avenue for a statutory-innocence claim risks making § 2255(e) largely superfluous and raises serious Suspension Clause concerns by denying a “meaningful opportunity” to show detention rests on an erroneous interpretation of law. Boumediene v. Bush, 553 U.S. 723, 779 (2008). Interpreting § 2255(e) to allow a narrow § 2241 pathway for such claims best reconciles § 2255(e) with AEDPA’s limits in § 2255(h) while promoting procedural fairness where the prisoner otherwise has no forum to test the conviction’s legality.
